svg.title: Nilpotent matrices determine which projective weights can move
svg.desc: A rank-one nilpotent line determines an ordered incident flag in three-dimensional vector space. A translation nilpotent plane has common kernel and total image of dimension two; its dual nilpotent plane has both of dimension one. The ordinary parameter equivalences and the additional polarity operation are displayed separately, including two self-dual four-dimensional parameters.
svg.text: The intrinsic flag fixes the order of the weights
All matrices below are represented by their unique traceless parts in sl₃(ℂ).
A nilpotent line ℂN, N = E₂₃
D(a,c) has ordered weights c on L, a on P/L, and 0 on V/P, before trace removal.
K₂(a,c) and F₄(a,c): [a:c] is exact under ordinary projective conjugacy.
Nilpotent rank and the Jordan part distinguish the exceptional rows
E = E₁₃+E₂₁: e₃ → e₁ → e₂ → 0; E² = E₂₃, E³ = 0.
A nilpotent plane containing this rank-two chain differs from U and U′.
The mixed rows Z₃ and Z₃′ have no semisimple matrix outside their nilpotent plane.
The diagonal families T₃ and W₃ always have such a matrix: D(a,c), (a,c) ≠ (0,0).
Duality is an additional operation, with explicit parameter action
F₄ is self-dual exactly at [a:c]=[1:0] or [1:2].
Distinct ordinary conjugacy types can be dual: K₂(1,3) and K₂(2,3) form one such pair.
One-dimensional distinct-eigenvalue lines have six parameter values from permuting three eigenlines.
Proof: Theorem 8.9 and Corollary 8.10. Worked examples: Solutions 11–12.
